scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Users on pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) and pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2) report they cannot
reach each other in either direction. Both hosts can still ping their
own gateways (10.0.0.1 and 10.0.1.1). The NOC insists the fabric is
healthy: every BGP session is Established, all routes are present on
every router, no interface has flapped, and all FRR daemons are
running. Identify what is silently eating the traffic.

injection.action: add a FORWARD DROP rule for pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 transit

post_inject_check.expect: 0% loss   (gateway still OK -- INPUT chain untouched)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: leaf_router_0_0 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 discards every forwarded
  packet with source in 10.0.0.0/24 and destination in 10.0.1.0/24.
  All pc_0_0 traffic must transit leaf_router_0_0 (its only gateway),
  so pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 packets die there. The reverse direction fails
  too, despite matching no rule on its way in: pc_0_1's echo requests
  ARE delivered to pc_0_0, but pc_0_0's replies (src 10.0.0.2, dst
  10.0.1.2) match the rule and are dropped -- a one-directional filter
  breaks bidirectional traffic. Routing and BGP are completely
  healthy; the drop is at the firewall layer. Local delivery to the
  gateway itself uses the INPUT chain, which is untouched, so both
  hosts still ping their gateways.
Localization: leaf_router_0_0
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule
  (-s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24) on leaf_router_0_0
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP` on
  leaf_router_0_0
scenario.fix_spec:
remove the DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 --
`iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP`

bonus-explains-asymmetric-drop: explains that the single directional rule (10.0.0.0/24 -> 10.0.1.0/24) also kills the reverse ping because replies match it

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fabric control plane is fine; the problem is in the data plane filtering on leaf_router_0_0. The affected component is the Linux netfilter/iptables FORWARD chain on that leaf. We found an explicit inter-subnet block: on leaf_router_0_0, iptables -S shows “-A FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP,” while default policies are ACCEPT. Packet counters confirm it’s actively dropping traffic: “Chain FORWARD … 12 pkts 1008 bytes DROP … 10.0.0.0/24 -> 10.0.1.0/24.”

Mechanism: Hosts can ping their own gateways because traffic to/from the leaf itself hits INPUT/OUTPUT (both ACCEPT). Any routed traffic between subnets traverses the FORWARD chain. Echo requests from 10.0.0.2 to 10.0.1.2 match the DROP and never leave the leaf. Even when initiating from 10.0.1.2, the echo-reply returning from 10.0.0.2 back to 10.0.1.2 is dropped by the same rule, so connectivity fails “both ways,” appearing symmetric to users.

Localization: leaf_router_0_0, iptables FORWARD chain (data-plane filter), not an FRR/OSPF/BGP issue. Kernel forwarding is enabled (ip_forward=1) and rp_filter=0, so routing would work absent this rule.

Root cause: a misconfigured iptables ACL on leaf_router_0_0 silently drops 10.0.0.0/24 → 10.0.1.0/24 traffic.

Corrective fix: Remove the rule and ensure it isn’t re-applied by config management. Example: iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP (or flush the FORWARD chain), then persist the clean state (iptables-save). Optionally add an explicit ACCEPT for inter-VLAN traffic if desired. Audit other leaves for similar filters.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly names the affected device as leaf_router_0_0 multiple times in the diagnosis.

per_axis.axis: must-recognize-filter-pattern: recognizes healthy routing + healthy BGP with silent forwarding loss as a packet-filter fault, not a routing fault
per_axis.rationale: The submission explicitly states routing/BGP are healthy and correctly identifies an iptables FORWARD DROP on leaf_router_0_0 as the silent packet-filter causing forwarding loss rather than a routing fault.

per_axis.axis: bonus-explains-asymmetric-drop: explains that the single directional rule (10.0.0.0/24 -> 10.0.1.0/24) also kills the reverse ping because replies match it

Proposes removing the specific DROP rule and persisting the change, which directly fixes the fault.

Investigation log contains explicit iptables rules and packet-drop counters on leaf_router_0_0 plus kernel forwarding/rp_filter checks and failed pings; the agent’s inferences that the FORWARD DROP is blocking inter-subnet traffic and that removing it will restore connectivity follow logically. The essential alternatives (routing, rp_filter, forwarding) were checked and ruled out.
